articles.title_orig: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill calls for Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell's resignation after investigation
articles.title_zh: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill calls for Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell's resignation after investigation
articles.content_orig:
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell — Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s handpicked No. 2 she once lauded as a “voice for the voiceless” — has resigned under the weight of a growing sexual harassment scandal that led to his boss calling for his ouster.
The first-term governor said Caldwell submitted his resignation Friday afternoon, a day after she publicly called on him to step down after an investigation substantiated claims of sexual harassment and “serious repeated violations of state policy, including ethical lapses.”
Caldwell, the former president of Centenary University, was accused of making sexual comments to an aide and using his position to try to score a promotion for his girlfriend.
But in a defiant interview, the embattled pol denied he was resigning over his scandalous behavior.
“I’m not resigning because of the report,” Caldwell told the New York Times . “It’s false. I’m resigning because I don’t want to be a distraction to the administration.”
“I’m supportive of the Sherrill administration,” he added. “I want her to be as successful as possible.”
Sherrill formally called for Caldwell’s resignation in a statement Thursday night, the same day an explosive 61-page ethics report detailing his creepy conduct was released, and gave him 24 hours to step down.
“I hold everyone in my Administration to the highest ethical standard. We all have a duty to follow our state ethics and harassment policy and our Code of Conduct. Anyone who violates these will be held accountable.”
Caldwell, 66, blamed race as a driving force behind the investigation, which was sparked by an anonymous complaint in May.
“Unfortunately, in this current political environment, false accusations, especially against people of color, seem to be commonplace,” he said at the time.
Caldwell’s shocking fall from grace stands in stark contrast to the high praise Sherrill heaped upon him during her run for governor.
In July 2025, Sherrill called him a “voice for the voiceless,” and someone who is “committed to New Jersey” when she tapped him to be her running mate against Republican Jack Ciattarelli.
“I’m proud to select Dale Caldwell as my Lieutenant Governor running mate because we share a commitment to public service and challenging the status quo,” Sherrill said at the time, lauding him for marching in Selma, Ala. with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
The voluminous report, based on a probe led by former New Jersey Attorney General Christopher Porrino, highlights egregious examples of Caldwell abusing his position including scoring pricey tickets for romantic conquests, securing his girlfriend a cushy state promotion and tasking his aides with finding him a “first lady.”
One of the worst accusations featured in the report occurred in April, when Caldwell, 66, hit on a staffer’s much-younger friend at an official event, then threw a tantrum in the back of his state vehicle after his advances were rejected, allegedly telling the aide, “you young women are looking for young sperm.”
Caldwell’s attorney, Thomas Calcagni, denied that his client made the stomach-churning comment.
Caldwell, who is divorced, allegedly tasked a staffer with finding him a “first lady,” and when she said no, he became “pushy” on the subject, the report said.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use expanded database for potential voter purges
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use expanded database for potential voter purges
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday permitted the Trump administration to use an expanded federal database containing citizenship information, as the president encourages states to purge people from voter rolls.
The justices, divided 6-3 on ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, granted an emergency request filed by the government after lower courts ruled that the Trump administration’s changes to the database were likely unlawful.
Critics have said the data is unreliable and could lead to U.S. citizens being kicked off the voter rolls.
But the court noted in its unsigned ruling that the National Voter Registration Act bars the broad purging of voter rolls in the weeks leading up to an election, which “limits the potential impact” of the decision this year. States can still make individualized queries about voters.
On the broader legal questions raised in the case, the court said that federal law requires the government to respond to requests from states for information about citizenship.
The lower court injunction “prevents the federal government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court said.
In dissent, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the government had not done enough to show that the lower court ruling needed to be blocked.
In her view, “the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” she added.
Various groups challenging the plan, led by the League of Women Voters, have argued that it violates several laws, including the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act.
The Supreme Court decision “puts millions of Americans at risk for being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database,” the groups said in a statement.
Conservative who have backed the administration’s efforts to tighten voting laws, welcomed the decision.
The ruling “just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls,” Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said in a statement.
The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE, was set up by Congress in 1986 so that government agencies could quickly determine someone’s immigration status when they applied for benefits like Social Security.
The Trump administration expanded SAVE after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in March 2025 that required agencies to take steps to better ensure that only U.S. citizens vote in elections.
The government expanded the database by adding information from the Social Security Administration, which enabled searches using Social Security numbers and allowed officials to do bulk searches.
After states started putting their voter rolls through the newly expanded system, some local officials noticed mistakes; many of the flagged registrants were newly naturalized citizens, according to reporting from ProPublica and The Texas Tribune .
Texas was one of the first states to put its full voter rolls — more than 18 million registrations — through the SAVE database last year. Just three people have been charged with voting illegally as a noncitizen.
A federal judge blocked the Trump administration plan, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reaching the same conclusion.
In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that the district court’s ruling “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections” by preventing the government from responding to state requests to verify the citizenship of potential voters.
Opponents argue the expanded database could force bureaucratic obligations on newly naturalized citizens who are asked to prove their citizenship after being flagged by the system.
Noncitizen voting is extremely rare. All states are required to conduct voter roll list maintenance under federal law, and states already have processes to identify any noncitizens who do accidentally make it onto the voter rolls.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi visit wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi visit wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.content_orig:
At the conclusion of Xi's visit, CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer if the leaders achieved anything new on artificial intelligence.
"I wouldn't say anything new," Greer said. I mean, we've established this this dialogue, AI dialogue with the Chinese, which really is when I think about it, I think of like the red phone between the Kremlin and the White House during the Cold War. And the AI dialogue at a minimum is an opportunity, if the sides feel like they have something they need to share, whether it's risks or other things, we can do it. Most important thing is having a channel."
Greer said there would be "another meeting on AI in the next month or so" although the agenda has not yet been set.
Though Mr. Trump declined to answer shouted questions from reporters about Taiwan during Xi's visit, U.S. ambassador to China David Perdue insisted there is "no change" in the United States' policy toward Taiwan.
" There's no change, no change in the Taiwan policy here," Perdue told CNBC Friday. "He's fully committed to the One China policy. We're committed to the Taiwan Relations Act, the three communiques, and the six assurances. Nothing has changed there. Of course, China has tried to coerce change in that regard. We're not changing the language. We're not changing our position there."
For the last stop of the Chinese leader's state visit, Xi, his wife and the Trumps toured the National Archives briefly on Friday afternoon.
National Archivist Bradford Wilson showed the leaders and their wives the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
Journalists were too far away to hear their conversation, but Mr. Trump did speak briefly to the press.
Asked about his meeting with Xi, the U.S. president said "everything" was accomplished during their meeting, although he didn't elaborate.
During a tea at the White House, Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit.
Through a translator, Xi said everything on their visit was "done to the highest order of perfection" with "thought in every little detail." Xi also said through a translator that he and Mr. Trump "are like two people who are charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations." Xi said they're adding "new substance" to that strategic relationship.
Xi said the two leaders were likely to see each other later this year at the APEC China summit in Shenzhen, and then again at the G20 summit of leaders in the U.S. The G20 is expected to take place at one of Mr. Trump's properties in Miami. Xi welcomed Mr. Trump for a state visit to Beijing in May.
Mr. Trump said he and Xi would be "speaking a lot," adding, "I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
The television pool reporter in the room asked Mr. Trump if he asked China to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but he ignored the question.
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Trump told Xi it's "unacceptable" for China to be helping Iran in any way with the war. Perdue acknowledged that China has been involved in some assistance that went to Iran directly or indirectly. He also said China has expressed a commitment to not help Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese entities provided satellite images of a base in Jordan to Iran ahead of deadly Iranian strikes that killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded others.
"This has been a continual conversation over some period of time," Perdue told Fox News' Bill Hemmer. "President Xi responded as you might expect. They talked about the U.S. interests. President Trump did a great job making sure that China knows that this is unacceptable. We've seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn't the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi."
Hemmer asked Perdue if that means that China would stop assisting Iran. Perdue said the U.S. has seen "movement" in that direction.
"That's what the commitment is," Perdue responded. "They assured us yesterday they are not doing that. We know that in the past that there was some intel and some potential parts that went to either directly or indirectly. But President Trump again made it very clear, this is unacceptable to us, to have any interaction with Iran with regards to the support of this war."
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."

articles.title_zh: Ed Sheeran concerts at Robert Kraft stadiums cancelled over weather
articles.content_orig:
Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-eastern France, on 30 August, 2026
Rapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made  onstage earlier this month.
"So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday.
The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.
Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoter, not by himself.
Everything we know about the Ed Sheeran and Macklemore controversy
In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now".
"What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."
Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences.
Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done."
Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October.
US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week.
"I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show
While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."
The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University.
After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.
Sheeran early on said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group.
His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity, and fans to express frustration. Ticket prices for the tour plummeted as well.
Sheeran addressed the controversy head-on during the start of his set in Philadelphia last week.
He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".
He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

articles.title_orig: A nor’easter is strengthening near the East Coast. These cities will be hit hard.
articles.title_zh: A nor’easter is strengthening near the East Coast. These cities will be hit hard.
articles.content_orig:
Millions of Americans are gearing up for a rare, multiday nor’easter that is set to start pummeling the Northeast with rain, wind and flooding Friday.
Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people along the East Coast as of Friday morning, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island.
The storm already brought gusty winds and early flooding across the Eastern Seaboard on Thursday, with rough waves pounding shorelines. Winds up to 65 mph are forecast, with the strongest winds expected through Saturday night on Long Island in New York and in New England.
Heavy rain bands — up to 4 to 6 inches — will hit the area Saturday and into Sunday, and winds will push water onto shore, with 1 to 4 feet of inundation expected.
Widespread 1 to 3 inches of rain is possible from the Interstate 95 corridor to the coast. The Jersey Shore, Long Island and coastal New England are the locations likely to see the highest rain totals.
Waves of 10 to 18 feet are expected, with coastal flooding forecasts of 1 to 4 feet depending on the area.
The system is expected to intensify as it moves north. It will come onshore around New Jersey.
On Friday, the nor’easter will intensify as onshore winds increase from Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, to Cape Cod, Massachusetts. By Saturday, rain will begin from the Jersey Shore to eastern Massachusetts and is expected to last all day.
Saturday will also feature the highest wind potential, with wind gusts that could reach 60 mph in coastal locations.
Rain will continue for the Northeast and New England on Sunday, as beaches continue to take a beating from the strong onshore winds.
The storm will still be spinning just off the coast Monday. While winds will be weaker, rain and beach erosion will continue.
Winds are expected to lead to travel delays and power outages into Monday.
Southeast New England faces the highest risk of power outages because of the strongest wind potential and top-heavy trees with leaves still on them.
As of Friday afternoon, before the rain started in some areas, three major music events set for this weekend had already been canceled, including the annual Global Citizen Festival held at Central Park in New York City.
“Due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City this weekend, we have made the difficult decision, in consultation with the City of New York and NYC Parks, to cancel this year’s Global Citizen Festival,” the organization wrote on social media .
“Safety has to come first,” Global Citizen added, noting that this is the first time the festival has been canceled in 14 years.
All Things Go , another festival that was being held at Forrest Hills Stadium in Queens this weekend, was also canceled due to the weather.
And Ed Sheeran had to cancel his Boston shows , scheduled for Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium, Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement.
Areas of New Jersey were already lashed by rough surf Friday morning, with videos showing waves crashing along the shore.
“The waves, the wave actions, the way it comes in, it just takes everything in its path,” said Mike Jones, the emergency management director for Upper Township, New Jersey. “And there’s really no way to stop Mother Nature.”
A full moon Saturday night is also expected to lift tides up to 5 to 6 inches.
One New Jersey resident told NBC News that to prepare for this weekend’s nor’easter, she closed up her whole house.
Outside Washington, abnormally high tides were seen along the Potomac River, inundating roads with floodwaters and leaving a popular Maryland music festival practically underwater. The first day of events was canceled in advance.
In North Carolina, winds greater than 50 mph have been recorded. A video showed a car in the state nearly swept into the ocean before a tow truck saved it.
Elsewhere in the region, emergency preparedness crews are cutting down trees and readying sandbags. Officials have warned of flooding in neighborhoods.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Nolo is barreling toward Hawaii with 80 mph winds. It is a Category 1 storm and is moving north at 5 mph. At some point over the weekend, it is expected to become a major hurricane, upgraded to a Category 3 or 4.
The storm is forecast to stay south of Hawaii, but the islands will still feel Nolo’s wrath. Heavy rainfall — up to 30 inches on the Big Island — and intense winds are already affecting the state. People in Hawaii are preparing for the worst, expecting catastrophic flooding.
Just last month, Hurricane Lala brought destruction to Hawaii’s Big Island, damaging more than 100 homes and stranding people without water and power.
In addition to dangerous surf and damaging winds, mudslides are a major concern in Hawaii.
As of Thursday night, stores were sold out of generators and gas cans. Shops were boarded up and blocked with sandbags. Schools were let out Thursday to give residents more time to prepare for the storm’s effects.
Nolo is expected to reach full strength sometime Friday night.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit
articles.content_orig:
Pontiff says artificial intelligence must remain at service of people in first official papal visit to country in 18 years
Pope Leo has warned against losing humanity in a “paradise of machines” as he addressed global concerns over the dangers of artificial intelligence at the start of a three-day visit to France.
“If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for people to be educated in ethical discernment, capable of seeing what is morally right,” he said in a speech at the Élysée.
At a second address on Friday, the 71-year-old head of the Catholic church insisted that new technologies must “remain at the service of the human person rather than becoming yet another instrument of domination and injustice” in remarks to a gathering at the Paris headquarters ⁠of the UN culture and education body, ⁠Unesco.
“Every science risks losing its proper meaning when pursued without ethics,” he said. “Certain artificial systems have even been given the name of our human faculty of thought: intelligence. At the same time, however, our ideas and relationships risk being impoverished by a process of dehumanisation.”
He added: “While intelligence is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and when deemed no longer productive, rejected and discarded.”
Leo also criticised world leaders who disrespect the ⁠rule of ⁠law, without naming individuals. “Instead of ​respecting ‌the law, ‌those in power invoke ‌it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself ‌as though it were a commodity to be ​bought and sold,” he said.
Leo, who became pope in 2025, ⁠has been critical of the direction ​of ​global leadership in ​recent months. He ​said ‌the world was “being ​ravaged ​by a handful of tyrants” last April.
The first official papal visit to France in 18 years comes as Emmanuel Macron’s decade in office draws to an end ahead of next spring’s French presidential election, for which the far-right, anti-immigration Marine Le Pen is polling high. Pope Francis did not make a full state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate and refused to join the inauguration of the rebuilt Notre Dame Cathedral in 2024.
After France passed legislation in June granting some adult patients the right to assisted dying , the pontiff said he was concerned by trends “that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death.”
A key moment of the three-day visit will be a giant outdoor mass on Saturday, led by the pontiff at Place de la Concorde.
The pope, whose paternal grandmother was born in France, on Friday urged Paris to remain a “tireless champion of peace” worldwide. On Monday, he will deliver a speech on European peace in the eastern city of Metz as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues into its fifth year.
Leo called on the world not to ⁠become indifferent to the pain caused by “the scourge of war”.
He told Macron and other French politicians: “I urge you ‘… never to grow resigned to the prospect of war or to ⁠consider it ‘inevitable’.”
Leo will also visit Lourdes, a pilgrimage site for Christians worldwide, where he will privately meet seven victims of clerical sex abuse. After some survivors’ groups suggested a larger number of survivors should have been canvassed, the Catholic church said the pontiff was seeking in-depth dialogue with individuals.
France’s Catholic bishops’ conference has agreed to provide compensation after a 2021 report estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over 70 years by priests or other church-related figures in France. The report described a “systemic” cover-up by church officials.
In recent years, further accusations have emerged, including against workers at the elite Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram , near Lourdes.
On his flight to Paris, Pope Leo told reporters they were welcome to cover him, as he responded to the Trump administration’s attempt to bar US media from the White House and affirmed the importance of journalists covering public figures.
Asked by a CNN reporter about Donald Trump’s attempt to bar CNN and other reporters, Leo said the media were welcome on his plane. “I am very happy that here, you are all welcome,” he said.

articles.title_zh: Manchester City found guilty on almost all Premier League charges relating to financial breaches - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges the club has faced regarding breaching Premier League financial rules, according a report in The Athletic.
The sanctions have not yet been decided, and City are expected to appeal, according to an article by The Athletic’s David Ornstein on Friday, who cited anonymous sources briefed on the matter.
Sanctions could include points deductions, financial penalties, and even stripping titles won by City and relegation from the Premier League.
A spokesperson for City, who have denied the charges, said, “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.
“The club have diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”
Since a 2008 takeover by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family, City have been transformed from also-rans into the Premier League’s dominant force.
Eight of the club’s 10 league titles have come in the past 15 seasons, plus a first and only Champions League in 2023.
The club has been accused of breaching financial rules while on the rise to their current status.
Of the 115 charges, 80 are for breaches of regulations from 2009 to 2018, while the remaining 35 relate to failing to cooperate with the Premier League’s investigation.
The charges stem from leaked documents published by the German news magazine Der Spiegel in 2018.
Emails purportedly sent between top City executives showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from the UAE state-controlled airline Etihad and telecommunications firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group as income.
Other documents claimed to show off-the-books payments to then-manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.
City have insisted there is a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence” to prove its innocence.
They have already defended their position in one case in which a two-year ban from the Champions League by UEFA was overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in 2020.
The CAS found most of the alleged breaches of overstating sponsorship revenue were either not established or “time-barred” because they fell outside the five-year statutory limit for prosecution.
But no such time limitation clause exists in the Premier League case.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.
A severe punishment would also raise doubts about the future of City’s cast of star players, including prolific striker Erling Haaland.
Other clubs could make a claim for titles to be stripped and compensation if City gained an unfair advantage by proscribed means.

A view of the exterior of a Costco Wholesale store with rows of shopping carts lined up in the foreground and the warehouse-style retail building under a cloudy sky. (Photo: Cheng Xin, Getty Images)
(Photo: Cheng Xin, Getty Images)
BY KIRO NEWSRADIO NEWSDESK
Costco revealed it has received $184 million in tariff refunds from the federal government, with more money expected.
According to The Seattle Times , the Issaquah-based retailer said it’s putting the refunds toward lower prices on everyday products and nonfood items.
Costco reported nearly $96 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, up 11% from a year ago. Net income rose 15%.
In a defeat for the Trump administration, a federal judge in New York ruled in February that companies that paid tariffs struck down last month by the Supreme Court are due refunds.
Judge Richard Eaton of the U.S. Court of International Trade wrote that “all importers of record” were “entitled to benefit” from the Supreme Court ruling that struck down sweeping double-digit import taxes President Donald Trump imposed last year under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
The Supreme Court found those tariffs to be unconstitutional under the emergency powers law, including the sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs he levied on nearly every other country. The majority ruled that the president could not unilaterally set and change tariffs because taxation power clearly belongs to Congress.
The federal government collected more than $130 billion in the now-defunct tariffs through mid-December and could ultimately be on the hook for refunds worth $175 billion, according to calculations by the Penn Wharton Budget Model.
Eaton was ruling specifically on a case brought by Atmus Filtration, a Nashville, Tennessee, company that makes filters and other filtration products, claiming a right to a tariff refund.
All goods that go through U.S. Customs and Border Protections enter a process called “liquidation,” when the agency issues its final accounting of what is owed. Once liquidated, importers have 180 days to formally contest the duties. After that window closes, the liquidation is legally final.
The judge ordered customs to stop collecting the IEEPA tariffs the Supreme Court struck down last month on goods going through the liquidation process. And if the goods were past that part of the process, the agency would have to recalculate them without the tariffs.
“This is a great decision for importers and consumers who paid,” said Barry Appleton, a law professor and co-director of New York Law School’s Center for International Law. “It will make customs brokers busy. It should make things easier for the courts — and get a process underway for those importers who paid within the last 180 days.”

articles.title_orig: Rep. Thomas Massie: Trump 'comeuppance' will happen on Election Day
articles.title_zh: Rep. Thomas Massie: Trump 'comeuppance' will happen on Election Day
articles.content_orig:
Seen on a screen below an exit sign, President Trump speaks on the first day of the 2026 Republican convention on Sept. 9 in Dallas. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption
There's a rare thing happening inside President Trump's Republican Party: dissent.
The president has long insisted on loyalty, but in recent weeks, a growing number of Republican candidates and elected officials have distanced themselves from core pieces of his agenda: from calling for an end to the U.S. war with Iran and relief from high prices, to criticizing his handling of key agenda issues like immigration.
It comes at a critical moment for the GOP. With less than 40 days until voting ends, the party is scrambling to hold onto a slim majority in Congress, where control of both the Senate and House of Representatives could come down to just a handful of toss-up races.
Trump's presence in the midterms looms large. He has repeatedly told voters to vote like he is on the ballot , despite facing historically low approval ratings . That could backfire, according to the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll , which finds that a plurality of registered voters, 45%, and a majority of independents, view their vote as a vote against Trump.
"Trump's strength has always been primarily devised from his relationship to the voters," said Sarah Longwell, a GOP strategist and longtime critic of the president. "Republicans have always been loath to cross him because of his sort of stronghold on the party."
However, as Americans continue to sour on the president, Longwell argued that GOP lawmakers and candidates alike may "feel more comfortable bucking him on things that they really care about."
While most of the Republicans who have distanced themselves are on the ballot this fall, the splits have not been solely confined to the campaign trail.
On Tuesday, Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, who isn't up for reelection until 2030, released a letter urging the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate the president's son, Donald Trump Jr., after ProPublica reported that a Russian oligarch financed large portions of a lavish party to celebrate his wedding.
Though past Trump-critics have largely been voted out of Congress or left the party, and the president still enjoys overwhelming support from Republican voters, Longwell sees Curtis' move as a potential indicator that lawmakers view the president's coalition as increasingly fragile.
"You are starting to see the very beginnings of people recognizing that Trump just doesn't have the juice that he once did and starting to push back."
In poll after poll, Americans consistently rank the cost of living as their top concern, and now, many say the conflict has added additional financial strain on their lives.
It's a connection that some Republican candidates running in toss-up races this cycle are acknowledging. On Monday, two GOP Senate candidates – Ashley Hinson of Iowa and Mike Rogers of Michigan – came out against the war and lobbied for additional relief for Americans impacted by rising costs.
"Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran," Hinson said in a statement on X , adding the conflict "needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end."
The comments marked a shift for Hinson, who has previously voted against efforts to end the war .
In a video filmed at a supermarket, Rogers also made a point to link rising prices to the conflict.
"Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down. The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly. When it does, energy costs will plummet," he said.
Neither Hinson nor Rogers directly mentioned Trump in their statements, but their comments marked a clear break with the White House, given Trump has consistently defended his decision to go to war with Iran and has downplayed the conflict's effect on the economy.
There appears to be growing impatience with the war on Capitol Hill too. Just last week, seven House Republican lawmakers — up from four over the summer — joined Democrats in supporting a resolution aiming to remove U.S. forces from Iran.
"For a long time, Republicans have stuck with the president through thick and thin. But the ones who are facing real trouble at the polls need to differentiate themselves," said Ron Bonjean, a GOP strategist and founder of the public affairs firm ROKK Solutions.
By choosing to cross Trump this late in the election cycle, Bonjean said it underscores how high the stakes are for Republicans.
"They're doing everything they can to make sure voters understand that they're much more independent than voting with Trump 100% or agreeing with him 100% of the time," he added.
That independence could prove crucial for Republicans whose political fate may be determined by some of the same key voting blocs that moved right two years ago and have since distanced from Trump, namely, Hispanic voters.
Even in red states like Texas and Florida, House districts with large Hispanic populations have seen drops in Republican support, according to a recent New York Times/Siena poll .
That includes Florida's 27th district, where Rep. María Elvira Salazar is running to represent parts of Miami for a third term.
Last week, she released an ad directly criticizing Trump's immigration agenda, arguing his enforcement efforts have "gone too far."
"Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy," said Salazar, whose district is rated by the Cook Political Report as likely Republican. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
Like many Republicans, Salazar is still walking a fine line. In an interview with CBS News days after releasing her ad, she acknowledged having a "fantastic conversation," with Trump and described him as "very receptive."
"There are no attacks here," she added. "I'm just forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the South Florida area that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture."

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Nolo, a zig-zagging storm, threatens Hawaii with flooding rains
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Nolo, a zig-zagging storm, threatens Hawaii with flooding rains
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Nolo is seen approaching Hawaii's islands, in this satellite image captured Friday. Nolo is expected to avoid making landfall as it strengthens, but forecasters warn it will bring dangerous flooding rains. NOAA/NESDIS/STAR/GOES-West hide caption
People on the Big Island of Hawaii are under a hurricane watch Friday morning, as Hurricane Nolo moves over the Pacific Ocean toward the Hawaiian archipelago. The alert means hurricane conditions are possible within 24 to 36 hours. By then, the storm will likely be a major hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
Nolo isn't expected to make landfall this weekend, but it has two dangerous qualities: slow movement and heavy rain . Maximum rainfall amounts from the storm in some areas could top 2 feet, forecasters say, with totals of 10 to 25 inches expected more widely.
"This rainfall could produce catastrophic life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the NHC said in its public advisory.
As of Friday morning, Nolo's maximum sustained winds were at 105 mph, making it a Category 2 storm, and it was moving at only 5 mph. It's now moving north-northeast and is expected to slow to a crawl before turning toward the west and picking up forward speed on Saturday and Sunday.
But it will continue to build strength from warm ocean waters. Over the next 72 hours, Nolo's winds could top out at 140 mph, according to the forecast discussion , making it a Category 4 storm.
A forecast cone shows the expected movements of Hurricane Nolo as it approaches the Hawaiian archipelago. NOAA/National Weather Service hide caption
The heaviest rains will likely fall on the Big Island's eastern and southern areas, forecasters say. Neighboring Maui is under a tropical storm watch and could see up to 10 inches of rain.
Hawaii and Maui counties have opened shelters to people and pets, according to Hawaii Public Radio , which also reports that schools and government offices began closing on Thursday in preparation for the storm.
Nolo's path over the water has been prone to sudden shifts. Earlier this week, it was heading west across open ocean when it took an abrupt right-hand turn, sending it north directly toward the Big Island.
The cyclone is the latest in a busy hurricane season in the Pacific, where warm water is feeding a powerful El Niño phenomenon that's sparking storms and reshaping weather patterns around the world. The Pacific region has already seen three Category 5 hurricanes: Genevieve, Lowell and Polo.
Nolo brings torrential rains to Hawaii weeks after the state endured flooding and wind damage from three other big storms. Hurricane Lala raked the Big Island, Maui, Oahu and Kauai at close range in mid-August, followed by Tropical Storm Moke one week later . Then Hurricane Lowell pummeled Kauai and other areas in early September.
Three hurricanes are spinning in the Pacific Ocean, as seen in this satellite image from Friday morning. In the west, Nolo is bringing rain to Hawaii while to the east, Hurricane Odalys grows over open water. Further east, the powerful Hurricane Polo is threatening Baja California Sur. hide caption
Nolo's growth represents a reversal: Last week, forecasters declared the system was dissipating and would not merit further updates unless it regenerated -- and that's precisely what it did. Days ago, the NHC renewed issuing advisories of Tropical Depression Fifteen-E and warned that it could strengthen quickly. It then became Tropical Storm Nolo before intensifying into a hurricane.

Hurricane Polo has regained its strength to a Category 5 storm and is moving away from Mexico's western coast, but is forecast to make a turn and make landfall in Baja California Sur and then mainland Mexico next week.
According to the latest update from the National Hurricane Center , Polo is about 280 miles southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico, with maximum sustained winds around 180 mph with higher gusts.
Forecasters said Polo is moving west at around 12 mph, with this motion expected to continue through Friday, followed by a gradual turn to the northwest Saturday and north on Sunday. On Monday, Polo is expected to turn toward the northeast and approach Baja California Sur.
Swells generated by Polo will affect portions of the coast of southwestern Mexico during the next couple of days, forecasters said, and will then spread northward along the coast of west-central Mexico and toward Baja California Sur on Friday and into the weekend. The swells will likely cause life-threatening surf, rip currents and coastal flooding.
The hurricane center said Polo's intensity could fluctuate over the next 12-24 hours, with weakening beginning by Saturday. Moisture from Polo, however, could have impacts all the way in the southwestern United States, according to forecasters.
The moisture from the hurricane "may indirectly contribute to a heavy rainfall and flash flood threat in the region," the hurricane center said.
The exact location of the rain will depend on the storm's track, according to AccuWeather , but parts of Texas and New Mexico may feel the impacts next week. At the same time, a non-tropical storm moving across the western United States may interact with the hurricane's moisture, increasing the threat, the outlet reported.
"Depending on Polo’s track and how much of the storm remains intact, heavy rain could extend from Texas’ Big Bend region northeastward into central and eastern Oklahoma," AccuWeather reported. "Parts of the Texas Hill Country and areas farther east could also be affected."

New Taylor Swift music means it’s time to play every Swiftie’s favorite game: Who’s She Talking About? Swift released The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore on Friday, a deluxe version of last year’s album with four new tracks. The lead single, “Patient Zero,” is about Swift welcoming a woman with open arms after she got screwed over by one of the singer’s exes. So, say it with me: Who’s! She! Talking about!
The most likely answer seems to be Sophie Turner. If you’ll recall, shortly after Turner announced her divorce from Joe Jonas in 2023, she and Swift were photographed arm in arm going out to dinner twice in the span of 72 hours. What could they have been talking about? Swift also dated Jonas in the summer of 2008 and later told Ellen DeGeneres he broke things off with a 25-second phone call. An old wound, sure, but perhaps one that never healed?
“If you wanna party with somebody who might know / About the devil on his shoulder under his halo,” Swift sings on “Patient Zero.” She might have just left out the part where they were partying over a plate of spaghetti at Via Carota.
According to Swift, the inspiration was a little less specific. She told the U.K.’s Capital FM this morning that she got the idea for the song after dinner with a bunch of friends. “One of my friends told us that she had been reached out to by the new girlfriend of an ex of hers, asking for guidance on if she had had the same experiences with this guy that this new girlfriend was having,” Swift said. “And everyone in our group just immediately started saying like, ‘Oh, I’ve been through that too,’ and telling stories of when this kind of reach-out had happened for them.”
Swift said she thought this was “an interesting kind of angle on humanity and relationships” and was inspired to write a song “from the perspective of getting this phone call, and really only from the perspective and the side of the phone call of the ex who’s been through it before.”
While I’m sure that’s true to an extent, isn’t it more fun to believe that “Patient Zero” is joining “Forever and Always” and “Better Than Revenge” on the list of songs Swift has written about Jonas? I thought that list was over, but maybe the book is never closed on any of Swift’s former paramours. Besides, I’ll take that over a song about Cleveland any day.

articles.title_orig: Block the Merger Coalition Asks Court to Reject Paramount’s Settlement With States Over Warner Bros. Deal
articles.title_zh: Block the Merger Coalition Asks Court to Reject Paramount’s Settlement With States Over Warner Bros. Deal
articles.content_orig:
A coalition of groups under the Block the Merger banner have filed an amicus brief – a third party representation in a court case – opposing the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery merger.
The brief was filed late Thursday by Free Press, the Committee for the First Amendment, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, the Future Film Coalition and the International Documentary Association in the federal court of California.
Earlier that day Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, who is presiding over the case, gave interested parties permission to file amicus briefs with a deadline of 12:01 a.m. PT on Sept. 25 after the Block the Merger groups filed an emergency motion requesting leave to file. The legal move came after 12 state attorneys general reached a settlement over proposed legal action over the merger.
“Since the terms of the consent decree were announced on Monday morning, few outside of those with a financial interest in this deal have suggested that it addresses the harms to competition, creativity, and independent journalism this merger will cause for years to come. The deal has been met with silence, skepticism, or tepid support at best,” the groups said in a joint statement.
“The arguments laid out in this brief reflect the concerns that just days ago, California Attorney General Bonta also willingly voiced. While we may never know what caused the radical turnabout to deliver such a toothless settlement, we do know that this consent decree bucks governmental safeguards designed to protect the public from harm. The court should reject it outright.”
The League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) has also filed an amicus brief against the settlement.

articles.title_orig: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.title_zh: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.content_orig:
The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.
In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.
But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.
Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case.
It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".
The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".
It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.
In a press briefing on Friday , European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.
He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.
In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.
Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability".
"Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms.
"The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X.
"The days of censoring Americans online are over."
His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".
The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.
The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.
However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people.

articles.title_orig: ‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall
articles.title_zh: ‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall
articles.content_orig:
Republicans in Florida are growing uneasy as polling shows the deep red state is in play for Democrats in key races.
Former Republican Rep. Carlos Curbelo says the party is “bracing for the worst” in the adopted home state of President Donald Trump, which he won by 13 points in 2024.
Curbelo, a two-term Republican congressman who lost his House seat during a blue wave that rocked Republicans in the midterm election of Trump’s first term, tells Politico that he sees similarities to eight years ago.
“It’s definitely 2018 vibes out there,” he said. “A lot of former colleagues are bracing for the worst.”
Curbelo, 46, does not expect Florida Republicans to be wiped out—but the situation is growing grimmer by the day for his party.
“I still bet on Republicans holding the governor’s mansion, but it’s going to be more competitive than people could have anticipated just a few months ago,” he said.
Even former congressman Matt Gaetz’s father, Republican state Sen. Don Gaetz, is expressing concern.
“Anybody who is on the ballot ought to be concerned if they have a Democratic opponent,” he told Politico.
Decision Desk HQ moved the Florida gubernatorial race—between the ultra-MAGA Rep. Byron Donalds, who scored an early endorsement from Trump, and Democrat David Jolly—to be a “toss-up” this week. That comes a month after the Cook Political Report moved the race from “solidly Republican” to “lean Republican,” highlighting how fast things are deteriorating for the GOP.
Such a shift would have been inconceivable last January, when Trump returned to Washington after sweeping every swing state and winning Florida by nearly 1.5 million votes.
Trump officially endorsed Donalds to be Florida’s next governor on Feb. 20, 2025—when a YouGov poll pegged Trump’s approval rating at 50 percent. Now, amid war with Iran and a gallon of gas costing $4.42 in Florida, the latest YouGov survey puts his approval at just 33 percent.
In recent weeks, Florida Republicans have shown both subtle and not-so-subtle distancing from Trump and MAGA. Donalds pulled some photos and references to Trump that were plastered across his campaign website. He also cut down the mentions of Trump’s endorsements, even as a campaign official argues that Trump’s endorsement is worth its weight in gold.
Florida Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar was much more explicit. The Miami Republican, who represents a majority-Hispanic district, dropped a blistering campaign ad she filmed at the White House. The Trump-endorsed lawmaker called out Trump’s inhumane migrant crackdown as “going too far.”
Whether momentum translates to actual wins for Democrats in a state as red as Florida remains to be seen. Politicos have pointed to Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ redistricting—meant to win the GOP more seats in Congress—as potentially backfiring by spreading Republican votes too thin, something Florida Politics publisher Peter Schorsch has said is a “Dummymander.”
“I don’t think we are dead yet,” a GOP county chair in Florida told Politico. “We are not on life support. But we are hemorrhaging. The question is: Do we stop the bleeding now, or wait until we reach critical conditions?”

articles.title_orig: Susan Sarandon, Hannah Einbinder among more than 100 detained during anti-Netanyahu protest outside UN
articles.title_zh: Susan Sarandon, Hannah Einbinder among more than 100 detained during anti-Netanyahu protest outside UN
articles.content_orig:
Award-winning actress Susan Sarandon and Hacks star Hannah Einbinder were among dozens of protesters detained Thursday in New York during a demonstration against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as he visited the United Nations .
NYPD said it took 103 people into custody as it tried to break up a group participating in a sit-in protest on First Avenue, just a few blocks from the UN headquarters, ahead of Netanyahu’s remarks to the UN General Assembly .
Video from the scene showed officers zip-tying Sarandon and Einbinder’s hands and directing them toward an NYPD bus.
Palestinian leader and Israeli PM relay two very different messages at UNGA
Meanwhile, protesters can be heard chanting with many wearing shirts that say, “Fund people not bombs,” and holding signs that say “Stop arming Israel” and “End the genocide.”
Comedian Caleb Hearon, author Glennon Doyle, New York congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier, and former Army intelligence analyst Chelsea Manning were also among those detained, according to Jewish Voice for Peace, a human rights organization that advocates for Palestinian rights and held the protest.
Other celebrities seen at the demonstration were actress and political activist Cynthia Nixon, playwright Tony Kushner, photographer Nan Goldin, and poet Eileen Myles. Congressional candidate Brad Lander also participated.
Jewish Voice for Peace said it held the sit-in outside the UN to “call on the world to stop arming Israel and to end the genocide in Gaza.”
A CNN team on the ground saw a heavy police presence with demonstrators remaining peaceful, but blocking traffic.
NYPD officers were seen arriving after 12 p.m. and warned demonstrators to clear the street. Around 30 people remained sitting and standing on the street, the CNN team saw.
What world leaders are doing in NYC during UNGA week
After another warning, officers began detaining protesters at around 1 p.m.
During his address Thursday, Netanyahu’s remarks prompted polarized reaction, with a large number of diplomats walking out of the room. The Israeli leader defended Israel’s military actions in Gaza and responded to international criticism, claiming if he hadn’t attacked Iran, “We’d all be dead.”
Last year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza since October 7, 2023, when Hamas carried out deadly attacks on Israel and Israel launched its military campaign. The Israeli government has maintained it is conducting the war in Gaza in self-defense and in accordance with international law, firmly denying accusations of genocide.
The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu, former Defense Minister Yoav Galland and a senior Hamas official, accusing them of war crimes. Netanyahu has dismissed the warrant as “absurd” and “antisemitic.” (The US is not a member of the ICC)
After Netanyahu’s remarks, hundreds of protesters also marched through the streets of New York with some chanting “Free Palestine,” “Gaza,” and “Netanyahu, you can’t hide. We charge you with genocide.”
Sarandon has long-been a prominent supporter of Palestinian rights and has widely condemned Netanyahu and Israel’s war in Gaza. CNN has reached out to Sarandon’s team for comment.
In a story on Instagram , Hannah Einbinder acknowledged her detainment, writing, “If the pictures of my friends and me getting arrested in protest of Netanyahu’s shameful visit to New York draw attention to anything, let it be to the devastating genocidal war is waging against the people of Palestine and Southern Lebanon.”
Hearon also posted to Instagram , where he thanked the protest organizers and said he was out of jail.
CNN’s Jeff Winter and Brynn Gingras contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Nepal’s leader labels devastating flood a ‘warning to the world’
articles.title_zh: Nepal’s leader labels devastating flood a ‘warning to the world’
articles.content_orig:
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah has appealed for action to combat the rising threat of climate change, calling the flood that devastated his country last month “a warning to the world”.
Shah made the comments during his address to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday night. He told the gathering that the August disaster “was not just a local tragedy”, asking them the question, “Have you really heard that warning?”
Political leaders “have been negligent to translate those warnings in action at the speed and scale that the vulnerable people require,” he said.
At least 1,453 people died when a torrent of mud, rock and water struck northern Nepal and the China-Tibet border on August 26, triggered by a glacial collapse.
According to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 5,500 people were still missing and 13,795 had been rescued.
Researchers from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) group said in a report released last week that the disaster was not caused by a single extreme weather event, but rather a “compound crisis” shaped by long-term warming, glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and geological instability.
Shah said climate change was hurting people not responsible for the crisis but who “are paying a colossal price for it”.
He said Nepal contributed less than one-tenth of 1 percent of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. About 99 percent of the country’s electricity comes from hydropower, and many workers were trapped in tunnels by the flooding.
“Our glaciers are retreating, our mountain slopes are becoming unstable, our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development,” Shah said.
Shah urged the international community to help bear the cost of helping Nepal adapt to climate change.
He proposed to create a ‘Himalaya Climate Resilience Mechanism’ which would include Nepal and neighbours India and China, and would allow them to share satellite data and expertise, monitor glacial lakes and strengthen joint early warning systems.
Nepal has asked the UN’s loss and damage fund for $20m in aid, the maximum allowed, but a tiny fraction of what it needs. A preliminary assessment by the government has placed the cost of the disaster at $5bn.
The fund, established in 2022 in the aftermath of catastrophic floods in Pakistan, has yet to make even its first disbursement, and observers see Nepal as a key test of its credibility.
Earlier this week, the United States pledged an additional $31m in new flood recovery support.

articles.title_orig: The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century: A Printable List
articles.title_zh: The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century: A Printable List
articles.content_orig:
Despite critical acclaim, “The Wire,” the unflinching HBO crime series set in 2000s Baltimore, famously never won an Emmy Award and earned only two nominations during its five-season run.
This morning, more than 18 years after its conclusion, the TV show that became synonymous with the city it depicted received a posthumous bouquet of flowers from its industry peers.
“The Wire” was named No. 2 on The New York Times’ list of the 100 best TV shows of the 21st century , based on votes from hundreds of actors, showrunners and other TV industry experts. The television series, created by Silver Spring native David Simon, fell short of AMC’s “Breaking Bad,” the white-knuckle tale of a science teacher’s unlikely rise as a methamphetamine kingpin.
“It soars above the meticulous rigor of its parts and labor into a ‘dark corner of the American experiment,’” Pulitzer Prize-winning critic Wesley Morris wrote of “The Wire” in the final results. He also called it “a miracle that should never have worked,” in part because it was made by “white people dreaming up Black life.”
The fictional show illuminated the drug war’s often heartbreaking trickle-down effects on policing, schools, politics and those caught in the drug trade’s wake. While widely heralded, “The Wire” and its success have created a complicated relationship between the show and Baltimore . Its critics say the series’ laser focus on often violent drug crime and its cascading effects on a city presents a too-narrow vision of Baltimore to the rest of the world.
The top five also included “Mad Men,” the 1960s period drama created by Baltimore County native Matthew Weiner , at No. 3, “Succession” at No. 4 and “Fleabag” at No. 5.
George Pelecanos, a producer of “The Wire” who earned an Emmy nod for co-writing the Season 3 episode “Middle Ground” with Simon, said he was happy to see the series so high on the list. He had no issue with “Breaking Bad” at No. 1, but was also quick to call the rankings, and top lists in general, “kind of silly.”
“Let’s be honest,” Pelecanos said Friday morning. “It’s completely subjective, and I looked at some of the celebrity lists, and they’re naming their friends.”
More than 500 ballots were cast, according to The New York Times. A series had to have premiered on or after Jan. 1, 2000, to qualify — in case anyone is wondering why “The Sopranos,” which debuted in January 1999, didn’t make the list.
Having premiered on June 2, 2002, “The Wire” presented a sweeping, kaleidoscopic view of an American city ravaged by the war on drugs, seen through the eyes of a wide range of players entangled in a largely futile battle. The ensemble cast included Dominic West, Michael K. Williams, Wendell Pierce, Wood Harris and Sonja Sohn, along with future leading men like Idris Elba and Michael B. Jordan.
“The Wire” was never a huge ratings hit — the 2008 series finale was watched live by a little more than 1 million viewers, compared with 11.9 million for the end of “The Sopranos” the prior year, according to ScreenRant .
“It is one of those series, like the original ‘Star Trek,’ that future generations will refuse to believe struggled with low ratings during its entire run,” The New York Times’ James Poniewozik wrote in a glowing 2022 reappraisal .
But its stature and fandom have only grown as more viewers have discovered “The Wire” through binging DVD box sets and then the streaming revolution. One superfan, President Barack Obama, hosted Simon at the White House in 2015 to discuss the show’s major themes.
The series has its detractors as well. P. David Bramble, the Baltimore native and lead developer of Harborplace’s renovation, called “The Wire” a roadblock to raising money for one of Baltimore’s biggest redevelopment projects.
“If you’re ever trying to raise investment capital and you call anyone in New York, California, Chicago to try to get money, the first thing you hear is ‘Is Baltimore really “The Wire”?’ You hear that over and over again,” Bramble told the Baltimore Business Journal in April. “I got to tell you, getting over that hump of getting people interested in Baltimore is really, really hard.”
S. Rasheem, a social scientist, has presented her new Baltimore-focused documentary, “Beyond the Wire,” as a counter-narrative to the drug- and crime-infested national reputation “The Wire” helped create.
When “The Wire” was being filmed, actors like Andre Royo, who played the charming Bubbles, a character struggling with heroin addiction, could not have imagined the acclaim the show would later receive.
“I wanted to get my career poppin’ and, you know, raise my daughter with some money. I didn’t know that it was gonna impact like that. But, like I said, I’m humbled by it,” Royo told The Banner in late June.
Several cast members have died this past year. In May, Bobby J. Brown , who played a police officer, died at 62 in a barn fire in St. Mary’s County. In December, Isiah Whitlock Jr. , who played the indelible politician Clay Davis, died at 71, while James Ransone , who played the loose cannon Ziggy Sobotka, died at 46.
All five seasons of “The Wire” are available to stream with an HBO Max or AMC+ subscription.

articles.title_orig: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
articles.title_zh: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”
